title: Write and Deploy Your First Sigma Detection Rule
description: Write a Sigma rule to detect a common attacker technique, convert it to your SIEM's query language, and verify it produces an alert when the technique is simulated in your homelab.
objective: Students will write a working Sigma detection rule for a real attacker technique, convert it to SIEM query syntax, deploy it, and verify it alerts when the technique is executed in the homelab.

steps.title: Install Sysmon and Configure Logging
steps.instructions:
Sysmon gives you detailed Windows telemetry that basic Event Logs miss. Install it on your Windows VM:

**Download Sysmon:**
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon

**Download SwiftOnSecurity's config (best practice baseline):**
https://github.com/SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config

```powershell
# Install Sysmon with the config
Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig-export.xml

# Verify it's running
Get-Service Sysmon64

# Check events are being generated
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' -MaxEvents 10
```

Verify you can see EventID 1 (Process Create) entries. These are what your Sigma rule will target.

steps.title: Write the Sigma Rule
steps.instructions:
Create a file `detect_powershell_download.yml`:

```yaml
title: PowerShell Download Cradle Detection
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
status: experimental
description: |
  Detects PowerShell commands commonly used to download
  and execute payloads from the internet (LOLBin technique).
author: YourName
date: 2026/08/04
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_commands:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'IWR'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'IEX'
      - 'Invoke-Expression'
      - 'WebClient'
  condition: selection_process and selection_commands
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate admin scripts (document and whitelist)
  - Windows Update components (validate with full path)
level: high
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1027
```

Save the file. Verify the YAML is valid using: https://yamlchecker.com/

steps.title: Convert Sigma to Your SIEM Query
steps.instructions:
Use the online Sigma converter to translate your rule:

**Option 1 — Online (easiest):**
Go to https://sigconverter.io/
- Upload or paste your `.yml` rule
- Select your target: Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic, etc.
- Copy the generated query

**Option 2 — Command line (pySigma):**
```bash
pip install pySigma pySigma-backend-splunk

# Convert to Splunk SPL
python -c "
from sigma.collection import SigmaCollection
from sigma.backends.splunk import SplunkBackend
with open('detect_powershell_download.yml') as f:
    rules = SigmaCollection.from_yaml(f.read())
backend = SplunkBackend()
print(backend.convert(rules))
"
```

**Document the converted query** — paste it into your notes.

steps.title: Trigger the Detection
steps.instructions:
In your Windows homelab VM (isolated lab only!), run a benign command that would match your Sigma rule:

```powershell
# BENIGN TEST — downloads from a safe URL
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://www.google.com -OutFile test.html

# Another test pattern
$wc = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
$wc.DownloadString("https://example.com")
```

These are real patterns attackers use — you're confirming your detection works.

**In your SIEM (or Event Viewer):**
- Check Sysmon EventID 1 events
- Filter for `powershell.exe` in the CommandLine
- Verify the `Invoke-WebRequest` command was logged

```powershell
# Check Sysmon for your test
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' |
Where-Object {$_.Message -like '*Invoke-WebRequest*'} |
Select-Object TimeCreated, Message | Format-List
```

Take a screenshot showing the Sysmon event captured.

steps.title: Document and Share
steps.instructions:
Create a `README.md` in your detection-rules GitHub folder:

```markdown
## detect_powershell_download.yml

**Technique:** T1059.001 — PowerShell
**Severity:** High
**MITRE Phase:** Execution / Defense Evasion

### What it detects
PowerShell processes spawning with command-line arguments that indicate
a download cradle — a common technique used by malware loaders.

### How to test
Run in isolated lab: `Invoke-WebRequest -Uri https://test.com -OutFile out.txt`

### False positives
- Windows Update: whitelist `C:\Windows\System32\`
- Known admin scripts: document and exclude specific hashes

### Converted SIEM queries
- Splunk SPL: `[paste your converted query]`
- Microsoft Sentinel KQL: `[paste your converted query]`
```

Push all files to your GitHub portfolio:
```bash
git add detect_powershell_download.yml README.md screenshots/
git commit -m "Add PowerShell download cradle Sigma detection rule"
git push
```

expected_output: A working Sigma rule file (.yml) on GitHub, a screenshot of the Sysmon event captured when the test PowerShell command was run, and the SIEM query equivalents for at least one platform.
